lead: A firewall is a policy enforcement point. It sits between two networks and forwards only traffic that matches an ordered rule table. Each rule states a condition and an action, allow or deny. The first matching rule wins, and a final default-deny rule protects the rest. Firewalls exist because a network cannot trust every packet that arrives from the Internet or leaves for it. You meet them at home routers, in cloud security groups and in front of a company DMZ. This chapter covers rule tables, firewall types and common layouts.
prereq: You need: Unit 1 network attacks and port scanning, and Unit 5 VPN basics.

blocks.text: A firewall inspects each packet or connection at a boundary. The boundary can be between the Internet and a company LAN, between two internal subnets, or between a cloud network and the public Internet. The firewall applies a rule table in order. A rule has a match part and an action. The match part can name source address, destination address, protocol, source port and destination port. The action is allow or deny, often written accept or drop.

Order matters. The firewall compares a packet with rule 1, then rule 2, and stops at the first match. A broad allow placed above a specific deny hides the deny. Put specific rules first and a final default-deny rule last. Default deny means the firewall blocks anything not explicitly allowed. Default allow is unsafe because new services and mistakes pass without review.

items: Ingress filtering checks packets entering a network. Egress filtering checks packets leaving it.
Logging records time, source, destination, port, action and rule number. Logs support audit and incident response.
NAT translates private addresses to public addresses. It reduces direct exposure but is not a policy. Keep default deny after translation.
A stateless firewall needs rules for both directions. A stateful firewall records allowed connections and admits their replies.

blocks.text: A packet-filtering firewall, also called a screening router when it runs on a router, checks each packet against the rule table. It is fast and simple. It keeps no memory of earlier packets, so it needs a reverse rule for reply traffic. It cannot see application data inside a packet.

A stateful inspection firewall keeps a connection table. For a TCP connection, the table stores source, destination, ports and sequence state. When the server replies, the reply matches the table entry and is allowed without a separate reverse rule. The table has limits, so it can be exhausted by too many half-open connections.

An application-level proxy terminates the client connection and opens a second connection to the server. It can inspect HTTP, SMTP or DNS content and enforce user-level policy. It costs memory and CPU, and each proxied service needs support. A proxy hides internal hosts because the server sees the proxy address.

A next-generation firewall adds application identification, user identity and threat feeds to stateful filtering. Unified threat management combines a firewall with antivirus, intrusion prevention and web filtering. Only a few universities teach these details; keep the core idea: more inspection at the same policy point. IDS and IPS detail is in 6.2.

The layout decides where inspection happens. A dual-homed host has two network interfaces and forwarding disabled. It can act as a proxy between the Internet and the LAN. A screened host puts a firewall on a router and a bastion host behind it. A screened subnet places public servers in a separate network called a DMZ.

items: Screening router: packet filtering on the border router. Cheap, but one device carries all policy.
Dual-homed host: one host with two interfaces, no IP forwarding, proxy services. A single failure point.
Screened host: border router filters traffic, then a bastion host applies stronger checks.
Screened subnet: firewall allows web and mail into a DMZ, and allows VPN and web into the internal LAN. The internal LAN is not directly reachable from the Internet.

blocks.text: In a screened subnet, the DMZ holds servers that need public access, such as a web server on TCP 443 and a mail server on TCP 25. The firewall allows those ports to the DMZ and allows only selected traffic, such as VPN and TCP 443, to the internal LAN. A DMZ limits damage: if a public server is compromised, the attacker still faces the firewall before the internal LAN. Security policy work is in 6.7.

examples.question: A stateless firewall has rules in order: 1 allow TCP from 10.0.0.0/24 to 192.168.1.10 port 443; 2 deny TCP any to 192.168.1.10 port 23; 3 allow TCP any to 192.168.1.10 port 80; 4 deny all. State the decision for packets: (a) 10.0.0.5:50000 to 192.168.1.10:443, (b) 8.8.8.8:40000 to 192.168.1.10:23, (c) 10.0.0.5:50001 to 192.168.1.10:22.
steps: Packet (a): destination port is 443. Rule 1 allows TCP from 10.0.0.0/24; 10.0.0.5 is inside that prefix. The first match is rule 1, action allow.
Packet (b): rule 1 fails because 8.8.8.8 is not in 10.0.0.0/24 and the destination port is 23, not 443. Rule 2 denies TCP to port 23; the first match is rule 2, action deny.
Packet (c): rule 1 fails because the destination port is 22, not 443. Rule 2 fails because the destination port is 22, not 23. Rule 3 fails because the destination port is 22, not 80.
No allow rule matches packet (c). The firewall reaches rule 4, deny all. The first match is rule 4, action deny.
The deciding rule numbers are 1, 2 and 4 for packets (a), (b) and (c).
examples.answer: Packet (a) is allowed by rule 1, packet (b) is denied by rule 2, and packet (c) is denied by rule 4.

traps: Default allow is unsafe: an unlisted service passes. Use a final default-deny rule.
First match wins, so a broad allow above a specific deny hides the deny. Put specific rules first.
A stateful firewall keeps a connection table and admits replies to allowed connections. A stateless firewall needs a separate reverse rule.
NAT changes addresses and ports; it is not a firewall and does not replace default deny.
An application proxy terminates the client connection; a packet filter forwards packets. They inspect at different layers.

quiz.q: Define default deny in a firewall rule table.
quiz.a: Default deny means the firewall drops every packet that does not match an explicit allow rule. A final deny-all rule enforces it.

quiz.q: Name four firewall types or inspection styles.
quiz.a: Packet filtering, stateful inspection, application-level proxy, and next-generation firewall.

quiz.q: Why does rule order matter in a firewall table?
quiz.a: The firewall stops at the first matching rule. A broad allow placed before a specific deny lets the packet through, so the deny never runs.

quiz.q: Using the worked example rules, what is the decision for TCP 10.0.0.7:51000 to 192.168.1.10:80?
quiz.a: Rule 1 fails because the destination port is 80, not 443. Rule 2 fails because the port is 80, not 23. Rule 3 allows TCP to port 80. Decision: allow by rule 3.

quiz.q: A stateful firewall allows an outbound TCP connection from 10.0.0.5:50000 to 8.8.8.8:443. Does it need a separate inbound rule for the reply? Explain.
quiz.a: No. The firewall records the connection in its state table. The reply from 8.8.8.8:443 to 10.0.0.5:50000 matches that entry and is allowed as part of the established connection.

quiz.q: What is a DMZ and why place a public web server there?
quiz.a: A DMZ is a separate subnet between the Internet and the internal LAN. A public web server sits there so an attacker who compromises it still faces the firewall before reaching internal hosts.

quiz.q: Rules: 1 allow TCP any to 192.168.1.10 port 80; 2 deny TCP 203.0.113.0/24 to any; 3 allow all; 4 deny all. What happens to TCP 203.0.113.9:40000 to 192.168.1.10:80?
quiz.a: Rule 1 matches first: it allows TCP to 192.168.1.10 port 80 from any source. The packet is allowed. Rule 2 is never reached because first match wins.

beyond: Not for the exam. Cloud platforms turn firewall rules into security groups and network ACLs, so the same ordered-match thinking appears in console screens. Zero-trust designs add identity checks before a connection is allowed. Modern data-centre firewalls run in software using kernel packet hooks such as eBPF and XDP. Search for cloud security groups, zero trust network access, and eBPF firewall to go further.
